## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a06-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Interconnection queue</dt><dd>The line of requests to connect to the grid; a request waits for studies, upgrades and an agreement before it can run.</dd>
<dt>Cluster study</dt><dd>Every request in a window is studied together, and the network upgrades they need are split by each one's impact on the overloaded line.</dd>
<dt>Withdrawals</dt><dd>When a request leaves, the others' shares change and they are restudied: in this lesson, 150 more days and the wind farm's share from $215 to $343 per kW.</dd>
<dt>N−1</dt><dd>A substation is planned to carry its load with any one line out, so two 350 MW lines serve 350 MW, not 700 MW.</dd>
<dt>Requested is not connected</dt><dd>Of the capacity that asked to connect in 2000–2020, 13% was operating by the end of 2025.</dd>
<dt>Three accounts</dt><dd>A wait costs the developer, other customers and society different amounts. A tariff reallocates the utility's costs; earlier service and bridge power change costs differently across the accounts.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Splitting an upgrade by impact</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Each request $i$ of $m_i$ MW puts a share $d_i$ of its output on the overloaded line, its [distribution factor]{.lx-term term="distribution-factor"}: an added flow of $m_i d_i$ MW. An upgrade costing $U$ is split in proportion:

$$\text{share}_i = U \, \frac{m_i d_i}{\sum_j m_j d_j}$$

- **The sum** $\sum_j m_j d_j$ adds the line flow of every project still in the study, $j$ running over them.

| Request | MW | Flow on the line | Study 1 | Study 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ridge wind farm | 200 | 120 MW | $43.0M | $68.6M |
| Mill Road solar farm | 150 | 60 MW | $21.5M | $34.3M |
| Depot battery | 100 | 30 MW | $10.7M | $17.1M |
| Placeholder request | 250 | 125 MW | $44.8M | withdrew |

- **Per MW of flow.** $120M ÷ 335 MW = $358,209 per MW of line flow in study 1; ÷ 210 MW = $571,429 per MW in study 2.
- **Per kW installed.** The wind farm's $43.0M ÷ (200 MW × 1,000 kW per MW) = $215 per kW.
- **Real rules.** Order 2023's pro forma uses a proportional-impact method for network upgrades, but shares a substation's upgrades per request; study costs are split 10–50% per request and the rest by MW (MISO, slide 6).
- **Every project at full output** is this toy's single test; real studies test many conditions.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Order 2023's reforms, with their pro forma numbers</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

FERC issued Order 2023 on 28 July 2023 (184 FERC ¶ 61,054). Its pro forma rules, as MISO summarised them:

| Reform | Pro forma detail |
|---|---|
| Cluster studies | one study of all requests in a window: a 45-day request window, a 60-day customer engagement window, then a 150-day study, not counting facilities and affected-system studies |
| Site control | 90% at the request, 100% by the facilities agreement stage |
| Deposits | a study deposit by MW; at the agreement, 20% of the network upgrade costs |
| Withdrawal penalties | they grow with the time of withdrawal, based on study or upgrade costs; exceptions, such as a 25% cost increase |
| Late studies | penalties can apply after a 10-business-day grace period, capped at the study deposits, with exceptions: $1,000 a business day for a cluster study, $2,000 for a restudy, $2,500 for a facilities study; paid to the delayed cluster, not recovered through rates, not before the third cluster cycle |

- **Grid operators adapt them** in their own rules; ERCOT's market is largely outside FERC's rules.
- **Large loads** follow their utility's process, not Order 2023, which covers generators.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The ledger's present values, and staged service</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

CF7's toy discounts month by month, in three steps:

- **Monthly rate.** $i = (1+r)^{1/12} - 1$ with $r$ = 8% a year: 0.643% a month.
- **Annuity factor.** A cost $c$ in each of $\tau$ months is worth $c \, A(\tau)$ today, with $A(\tau) = \frac{1-(1+i)^{-\tau}}{i}$.
- **For 36 months,** $A(36) = 32.04$: 36 monthly costs are worth about 32 of them today.
- **Developer, 36 months:** lost margin $144.2M plus the carrying cost of idle capital $103.1M: $247.3M.
- **Other customers:** the upgrades' carrying cost $12.4M plus expected stranded upgrades $8.6M: $20.9M.
- **$L(t)$** is an account's present value when the whole load waits $t$ months.
- **Staged service.** Every part of the toy grows in step with the load, its capital and its upgrades, so a share $g$ connected at month $a$ gives $g\,L(a) + (1-g)\,L(\tau)$ in each account.
- **Half at month 12:** $0.5 × $88.8M + 0.5 × $247.3M = $168.1M for the developer.
- **The most worth paying** for a connection 12 months sooner is the cost it avoids: $247.3M − $171.1M = $76.2M, before other risks or costs.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Affected-system studies, when a project also loads a neighbouring grid, and facilities studies of the equipment at the connection.</li>
<li>Many operating conditions: the toy tests one, every project at full output; real studies test peak and light load, and faults.</li>
<li>Voltage, short-circuit and stability limits, which can bind before a line's thermal limit.</li>
<li>Permits, land, supply chains and construction crews, which set much of the time after the agreement.</li>
<li>Why the most a project would pay is what it is: here it is simply given.</li>
<li>What a large load does to a whole grid's plants, prices and adequacy: capstone <a href="c2-plains-grid-hard-year.html">C2</a> connects one to the Plains Grid.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>

## Check yourself

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a06-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="built" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Most of the capacity that asks to connect ends up operating.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Of the capacity that asked to connect in 2000–2020, 13% was operating by the end of 2025 and about 75% had withdrawn (Berkeley Lab).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="leaver" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A withdrawal only affects the project that leaves.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy, the placeholder's withdrawal raised the wind farm's share from $215 to $343 per kW and added a 150-day restudy. Order 2023 added withdrawal penalties for this reason.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="twolines" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A substation fed by two 350 MW lines can serve 700 MW.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With one line out (N−1), the other must carry everything: 350 MW. With the east side's own 150 MW, only 200 MW of new load fits.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="requests" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Large-load requests show how much new demand will arrive.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Of ERCOT's 474.7 GW of large-load requests, 284.3 GW had no studies submitted and 5.9 GW were energized (June 2026). Requests can be duplicates or placeholders.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a06">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="days" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">How long is a cluster study in Order 2023's pro forma rules?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">45 days</li><li data-value="b">150 days</li><li data-value="c">One year</li><li data-value="d">Five years</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>150 days, not counting facilities and affected-system studies. Before it come a 45-day request window and a 60-day customer engagement window.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="staged" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">In CF7's toy, a 36-month wait costs the developer $247.3M. Half the load is served at month 12 instead. What does the developer's cost become?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$247.3M</li><li data-value="b">$168.1M</li><li data-value="c">$123.6M</li><li data-value="d">$0</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$168.1M: half the load waits 12 months ($88.8M for the whole load) and half waits 36 ($247.3M), so half of each.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card a6-practice">
<!-- a06-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>Split an upgrade by impact.</b> A $120M upgrade is needed. Four requests put 120 MW, 60 MW, 30 MW, 125 MW of flow on the line. What does the 200 MW wind farm, with 120 MW of flow, pay?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$120M × 120 ÷ 335 = $43.0M, or $215/kW for its 200 MW.</p></details></li><li><p><b>After a withdrawal.</b> The 250 MW placeholder, which puts 125 MW of flow on the line, withdraws. Recompute the wind farm's share.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$120M × 120 ÷ 210 = $68.6M, or $343/kW: up $128/kW, and 150 more days of study.</p></details></li><li><p><b>N−1 with stronger lines.</b> Two 400 MW lines feed a substation whose own peak is 150 MW. How much new load fits before an upgrade?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>With one line out, the other must carry everything: 400 − 150 = 250 MW.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Security in Texas.</b> At $50,000 per MW, what security does a 120 MW load post for ERCOT's batch study?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>120 × $50,000 = $6.0M.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Present value of a wait.</b> In CF7's toy, lost margin is $4.5M a month, discounted at 8% a year, month by month. What is 36 months of it worth today?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$4.5M × 32.04 = $144.2M (the annuity factor for 36 months).</p></details></li><li><p><b>What a faster queue is worth.</b> Cut the wait from 36 to 24 months. What is the most the developer should pay for that?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Its cost falls from $247.3M to $171.1M: up to $76.2M, before other risks or costs.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Read a claim critically.</b> A headline says: “Texas needs 475 GW more power.” Name three questions you would ask.</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Are these requests or signed loads? How many are duplicates or placeholders? By which year, and against a peak of about 91.1 GW?</p></details></li><li><p><b>Match the reform.</b> A cluster keeps losing placeholder requests after each study. Which Order 2023 rule aims at that?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Site control and study deposits at the request (readiness), backed by withdrawal penalties.</p></details></li></ol>
<!-- a06-practice:end -->
</div>
```

<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>A late connection has a price, and someone pays it.</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:code"><p>A late grid connection costs the developer lost <span class="lx-term" data-term="margin">margin</span> and <span class="lx-term" data-term="carrying-cost">carrying costs</span>; ratepayers face utility carrying and <span class="lx-term" data-term="stranded-cost">stranding</span> costs; society bears <span class="lx-term" data-term="external-cost">external costs</span>.</p><p>The study keeps these present-value accounts separate.</p><p>The delay is treated as <span class="lx-term" data-term="exogenous">exogenous</span> and parameters are illustrative; network feasibility is not modeled, and the social perspective is illustrated with a single bridge-power example.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2026), accepted paper, 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS); DOI pending.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Holds when: the delay is given and the inputs are illustrative. Leaves out: why service is late.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">This lesson is about that last part. The full case: case file <a href="cf7-cost-of-waiting.html">CF7</a>; open code with illustrative inputs: <a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/code-delayed-energization">code-delayed-energization</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>

Queued Up: 2026 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission Interconnection As of the End of 2025. Berkeley Lab. <a href="https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/publications/queued-2026-edition-characteristics">Publication page</a>.</li>

Issue date and citation, slide 3; the 45-day request window, the 60-day customer engagement window and the 150-day pro forma cluster study, slide 5; network upgrade costs by proportional impact, slide 6; site control, deposits and withdrawal penalties, slide 7; penalties for late studies, with their cap, grace period and exceptions, slide 8. <a href="https://cdn.misoenergy.org/20230808%20IPWG%20Item%2004%20Review%20of%20FERC%20Order%202023629802.pdf">Slides</a>.</li>
